titleStmt.title: Design and Analysis for Dual Priority Scheduling

analytic.title: Design and Analysis for Dual Priority Scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper considers Dual Priority (DP) scheduling of constrained deadline sporadic tasks on uniprocessor. The initial fixed priority of each job of a task is promoted to a higher priority (called, promoted priority) after a fixed time interval (called, promotion point) relative to the release time of that job. DP scheduling alters the default preemptive behavior of traditional fixed priority (FP) scheduling to efficiently utilize the processor as close as possible to that of the optimal earliest deadline first (EDF) scheduler.

In this paper, we address some of the main challenges of DP scheduling including derivation of a sufficient schedulability test, determination of promotion point of each task 1 . To the best of our knowledge, this test is the first schedulability test for DP scheduling applicable to constrained deadline sporadic tasks. The test is applicable for any given promotion points of the tasks and has pseudo-polynomial time complexity. We also propose two different heuristics to assign the promotion points, and experimental results show that the proposed test achieves performance very close to that of EDF scheduling.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Priority-driven preemptive scheduling is widely used and a very popular scheduling paradigm for hard real-time sporadic tasks. The preemptive dynamic-priority based EDF algorithm is known to be optimal for scheduling such tasks on uniprocessor [12]: if there is an algorithm that can schedule a task set such that all the deadlines are met, then the task set is also schedulable using EDF scheduling. In contrast, the preemptive FP scheduling algorithm does not provide such a guarantee even under the optimal fixed priority assignment, for example, using deadline monotonic priority assignment for constrained deadline sporadic tasks [14]. Although EDF can fully utilize the processing capacity of uniprocessor platform, many practical systems implement FP scheduling due to its efficient runtime support [8], [16] or to comply with standards, for example, AUTOSAR [2] in automotive systems.

The real-time systems research community is continuously investigating how to exploit the full processing capacity of uniprocessor platform using some simple variations of classical fully preemptive FP scheduling algorithms without sacrificing their efficient runtime support feature. To that end, one group of studies, known as limited-preemption scheduling, considers executing some fraction of a task preemptively while the remaining fraction of the same task non-preemptively using FP scheduling algorithm, in order to achieve higher schedulability and/or to reduce the total number of preemptions (a survey on this topic can be found in [7]). Although limitedpreemption scheduling is effective in accepting larger number of task sets in comparison to fully preemptive FP scheduling on uniprocessor, simulation results in [7], [11] demonstrate that such strategies become less effective for task sets with very high utilization in comparison to that of EDF scheduling.

Another group of studies considers priority-promotionbased scheduling by tweaking the default preemption policy of traditional FP scheduling [5], [6], [9], [10], [13], [15]. Burns presented a conjecture in [5], [6] regarding the well known priority-promotion-based DP scheduling algorithm2 : all EDF schedulable constrained-deadline sporadic task sets are also schedulable using DP scheduling. Unlike the first group (i.e., limited-preemption scheduling), the second group (i.e., DP scheduling) has received considerably much less attention, even though it has the potential -if the conjecture is proven to be correct -to outperform all the limited-preemption scheduling algorithms proposed earlier.

The DP scheduling algorithm was first proposed by Burns and Wellings [5] in 1993. Under DP scheduling, each task has a fixed priority that undergoes priority promotion at a fixed time instant (called, promotion point) relative to the release time of each job. For example, consider task τ i that has (initial) fixed priority P with promotion point P i at which the priority of the task is promoted to priority level P such that P < P (lower priority value implies higher fixed priority). If a job of task τ i is released at time r i , the priority of this job is P at time r i and promoted to priority level P at time (r i + P i ). Other than priority promotion, DP scheduling is the same as traditional FP scheduling on uniprocessor.

DP scheduling introduces minimum dynamic-priority behavior to traditional FP scheduling by promoting the priority of each job only once. This enables efficient implementation of DP scheduling on a real-time kernel that already supports FP scheduling; a priority change primitive, standard in many commercial real-time kernels, is sufficient. Also, for practical systems that conform to standards requiring fixedpriority based scheduling, e.g., AUTOSAR, DP scheduling can offer significantly higher schedulability in comparison to FP scheduling with low additional implementation overhead.
DP scheduling can also be used with fixed-priority based communication protocols such as CAN in which messages are transmitted non-preemptively [6].
The main research problem of DP scheduling can be formally stated as follows:

Dual-Priority Scheduling (DPS) Problem. How to determine the promotion points and promoted priorities for each task of a set of constrained deadline sporadic tasks such that all the tasks meet their deadlines using uniprocessor DP scheduling? Davis and Wellings [10] studied DP scheduling to accommodate scheduling of soft real-time tasks with hard real-time tasks on uniprocessor. However, the analysis in [10] solves the DPS problem only for hard real-time task sets that are also schedulable using FP scheduling. In contrast, our research in this paper targets DP scheduling of those task sets that are not schedulable under FP but schedulable under EDF. Burns presented an approach in [6] to solve the DPS problem for implicit deadline tasks considering exactly n = 2 tasks, and the DPS problem for n > 2 tasks is still open. The only known solution of DPS problem for n > 2 is based on repeated simulation of DP schedule by exhaustively trying out in the worst-case all possible promotion points and promoted priorities [5], which is computationally infeasible. To tackle the DPS problem, we restate the DPS problem using two subproblems P1 and P2 as follows:

• (P1) How can we determine whether all the tasks meet their deadlines under uniprocessor DP scheduling for a given assignment of promotion points and promoted priorities for each task? • (P2) How to assign the promotion points, initial and promoted priorities to all the tasks? Considering the two subproblems P1 and P2, this paper has the following contributions. First, we solve P1 by proposing a sufficient schedulability test for DP scheduling for a given assignment of promotion points and priority assignment. To the best of our knowledge, our proposed test is the first schedulability test for DP scheduling applicable to constrained deadline sporadic tasks for any n (number of tasks in a task set).

Towards solving the second subproblem P2, we present heuristics to assign the promotion points for each task assuming a given set of initial and promoted priorities. Thus, our second contribution is proposing two effective heuristics to assign the promotion point to each task of a constrained deadline sporadic task set. The design of the first heuristic is guided by the philosophy that a task τ i 's priority must be promoted early enough so that one complete execution of one job of task τ i and one job of each task that has higher initial priority than that of τ i can take place after the priority promotion of τ i . The computation of promotion points is very simple and can be computed in polynomial time for all the tasks in a task system. The second heuristic is designed by tuning the first heuristic in order to achieve a relatively higher schedulability.

Finally, we also demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed schedulability test. Experimental evaluation results show that the proposed test of DP scheduling combined with the heuristic to assign promotion points is very effective. Its performance is comparable to that of EDF scheduling for some parameter settings, and it outperforms the state-of-theart limited-preemption scheduling [11] as well as optimal FP scheduling under all settings that we considered.

Related Work. Priority-promotion based DP scheduling was first proposed by Burns and Wellings [5] in 1993, and analyzed by Davis and Wellings [9], [10] considering shared resources, release jitter and for scheduling soft real-time tasks. The approach to solve the DPS problem in [5] simulates the DP schedule until the hyperperiod of a set of implicit-deadline periodic tasks by exhaustively searching (in the worst-case) all possible promotion points and promoted priorities.

Davis and Wellings [10] presented a strategy to schedule soft real-time tasks along with hard real-time tasks based on DP scheduling. A response-time test for each hard realtime task is computed by assuming that the processor has been continuously busy executing soft real-time tasks until the promotion point of the task. Unfortunately, the responsetime test in [10] is not satisfied for any task set that is not FP schedulable. Consequently, we cannot apply the test in [10] to solve the more general DPS problem considered in this paper.

There are many works on limited-preemption scheduling with the objective to reduce the number of preemptions in order to reduce context-switch overhead, tightly estimate the worst case execution time, and/or to improve the schedulability of traditional FP scheduling.

A survey on this topic can be found in [7]. The work by Davis and Bertogna in [11] presented an optimal algorithm for determining both the priority ordering of the tasks and the length of the final non-preemptive regions (i.e., the fraction of each task that executes non-preemptively). Simulation results in [11] show that the proposed approach outperforms all other limited-preemption schedulability tests proposed earlier. In summary, the work [11] is the state-of-the-art scheduling algorithm with limited preemptions. We have shown that our analysis of DP scheduling is more effective than the state-ofthe-art limited-preemption scheme.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the task model. In Sections III and IV, we derive the sufficient schedulability test for DP scheduling. We also propose an optimization technique for the test in Section V and present promotion point assignment heuristics in Section VI. In Section VII we present the evaluation results. Finally, conclusions are presented in Section VIII.

div.head: II. MODEL
div.p: In this paper, we consider the classic constrained deadline sporadic task model, where a task can be specified as the tuple: τ i = (C i , D i , T i , P i ). For each task τ i , the parameter C i denotes its worst case execution time, T i is the minimum inter-arrival time between two successive job releases, and D i ≤ T i denotes its relative deadline. Each job may execute up to C i time units within D i time units from its release time. Parameter P i denotes the relative promotion point of τ i under DP scheduling.
The k th job of task τ i is denoted by J k i . The release time, absolute promotion point, and absolute deadline of job J k i are denoted using r k i , p k i = r k i +P i , and
div.formula: d k i = r k i +D i respectively. In the interval [r k i , p k i )
div.p: this job is scheduled according to its initial priority, but its priority is promoted at time instant p k i and thereafter it is scheduled using its promoted priority.

Given a sporadic task system τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } with task indices sorted according to the initial priorities (a lower index denotes a higher priority), we assume that the priority of the tasks are assigned as follows:

Each task τ i has an initial priority (n + i) and a promoted priority i, where a lower number indicates higher priority. The above assumption is made to simplify the presentation in this paper. The proposed schedulability analysis framework for DP scheduling is generic enough so that it can be extended for any other promoted priority assignment (i.e., in violation of the above assumption). See discussion at the end of Section IV on how the analysis can be generalized.

div.head: III. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS FOR DP SCHEDULING
div.p: Consider a task system as defined in Section II. Suppose a task τ i is not schedulable using DP scheduling on a uniprocessor with the given priority and promotion point assignment. Thus, there exists at least one job release sequence in which a job of task τ i misses its deadline. Without loss of generality, we assume J L i misses its deadline at the end of a busy interval [0, t] (i.e., d L i = t), where a busy interval is defined as follows. Definition 1 (Busy Interval): Interval [t 0 , t] is defined as a busy interval if:
1) all jobs released before t 0 have completed by t 0 , and 2) a job is released at t 0 , and 3) there is no idle instant during [t 0 , t].

div.head: V. IMPROVED DP SCHEDULABILITY TEST
div.p: To improve the performance of the DP schedulability test in Theorem 1, we present an optimization technique in this section. Further, we also present an upper bound for the time instant t used in the test to show that the resulting test has pseudo-polynomial time complexity.

The general idea of the technique is very simple. Since the total execution time of jobs except J L i in the busy interval [0, p L i ] cannot exceed p L i on a uniprocessor platform, we can bound the total execution time of these jobs by p L i for the case when t > p L i . From Section IV, we know W i (τ j , t ) upper bounds the execution time of jobs of τ j during the busy interval [0, t ]. We now divide W i (τ j , t ) into two parts:

1) an upper bound of the execution time of τ j during [p L i , t ], denoted as W R i (τ j , t ), and 2) the remaining part W L i (τ j , t ) = W i (τ j , t )-W R i (τ j , t ). Thus the sum of W R i (τ j , t ) and W L i (τ j , t ) still upper bounds the the total execution time of τ j during [0, t ]. Now we use W R i (τ j , t ) to reduce the pessimism in W i (τ j , t ). div.head: VI. PROMOTION POINT ASSIGNMENT STRATEGY
div.p: The promotion point of each task has a significant influence on the schedulability of the system under DP scheduling. In this section we present two heuristics to assign the promotion points. We assume that the initial and promoted priorities of all the tasks are as defined in Section II.

Our first heuristic is based on the principle that each task must be promoted early enough so that at least one full execution of itself and one job of each of the higher initial priority tasks can be completed after the promotion. That is, for each task τ i we compute its promotion point as follows.
div.formula: P i = ⎡ ⎣ D i -C i - j<i C j ⎤ ⎦ 0 (14)
div.p: This heuristic, denoted as Execution-based Priority Promotion (EPP), can compute all the promotion points in linear time. To further improve the schedulability, we propose another heuristic algorithm to tune the initial values of P i obtained by EPP. We denote this heuristic as Execution-based Priority Promotion with Tuning (EPPT). The general idea of the algorithm is as follows. Once our test detects that τ i has a deadline miss at t, its promotion point P i is modified to P i -Δ i , where Δ i denotes step size. The value of Δ i controls the speed of this heuristic algorithm.

Suppose task τ i fails the schedulability test of Theorem 2 for some time instant t. If a task τ j has lower initial priority than τ i (i.e., j > i), then J L i which misses its deadline at t would not be interfered by a job J L j of τ j only if p L i ≤ p L j . Similarly, we can only reduce the interference of a job J L j of task τ j with j < i if p L i ≤ p L j . Thus, to eliminate the failure of the schedulability test for task τ i , we minimally advance its promotion point depending on p L i and the latest promotion point of the jobs of other tasks. That is, α t,i = min
div.formula: (τj ∈τ \τi)∧(p L i >p L j )
div.p: p L ip L j . Once we find that τ i is not schedulable, then α t,i could be used as a guidance to choose suitable values of Δ i . But if α t,i is very small (say 1) then the heuristic may take a long time to converge to a solution. Hence, we also set a lower and upper bound to limit the value of Δ i , i.e., Δ i ∈ α min i , α max i , where
div.formula: α min i = Di
div.p: x and α max i = Di y for any two positive integers x(≤ D i ) and y(≥ 1). That is,
div.formula: Δ i = min α max i , max α min i , α t,i(15)
div.p: In general, EPPT has pseudo-polynomial time complexity, because in the worst case the promotion point of a task τ i could decrease in steps of 1 from (D i -C i ) to 0. Note that tuning the P i parameter of one task τ i may cause a previously schedulable task to fail its deadline. Hence, once the promotion point of some task is tuned, we apply the test to all the tasks. Thus, the number of times we apply the test to all the tasks is bounded by O( n i=1 (D i -C i )), and hence the overall time complexity of the heuristic algorithm is also pseudopolynomial. In the simulation section we show that the number of tuning steps required to make a task system schedulable is relatively small.

div.head: VII. EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we present experimental evaluation of the schedulability test of Theorem 2 applied to the promotion point assignment algorithms EPP and EPPT.

The task sets we use in the evaluation are generated as follows. First we use the UUniFast [4] algorithm to generate a set of 10 tasks with total utilization equal to a desired value U . Then, for each task, its period T i is generated as a random integer uniformly distributed in the interval [50,200], and its execution time is computed as
div.formula: C i = u i × T i .
div.p: For constrained deadline systems, the relative deadline D i is generated as a random integer uniformly distributed in the range
div.formula: [C i + 0.5 × (T i -C i ), T i ].
div.p: In our experiments, we generate 1000 such task sets per value of utilization U , where U ∈ {0.6, 0.65, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95, 0.97}.

The initial priority of each task is assigned based on the deadline monotonic rule, i.e., a task with smaller relative deadline is assigned a higher priority. We choose x = 30 and y = 10 for step-size limits in EPPT. That is, α min i = D i /30 and α max i = D i /10. We compare EPP and EPPT against three other algorithms: fixed priority scheduling with optimal priority assignment denoted as FP [3], fixed priority with deferred preemption scheduling and optimal priority assignment denoted as (FPDS) (OPT) [11], and fixed priority with deferred preemption scheduling and deadline monotonic priority assignment denoted as FPDS (DM) [11]. As a reference, we also plot the optimal earliest deadline first scheduling policy for constrained deadline task systems denoted as EDF. Figure 6 shows the acceptance ratios3 of the algorithms for implicit deadline task systems. Note that for such task systems the optimal algorithm EDF can schedule any task set with U ≤ 1. As we can see, the acceptance ratio of EPPT is 100% for the randomly generated task sets that we considered; we have not yet found any task set that is not schedulable under EPPT. Although the acceptance ratio of EPP can not reach 100%, it also significantly dominates all the other algorithms.

In Table I we present the average and maximum number of steps EPPT took to converge for the implicit deadline task sets considered in the experiment corresponding to Figure 6. It is evident that the number of tuning steps is relatively small even for very large utilization values; the maximum observed number of steps is smaller than the number of tasks 10 in the task sets. For constrained deadline task systems the schedulability results are shown in Figure 7. Although the performance gap between EDF and EPPT (or EPP) becomes larger in this case, they (particularly EPPT) still outperform all the other strategies significantly for almost all utilization values.

The box-plot of Figure 8 shows number of steps EPPT took to converge for each constrained deadline task set considered in the experiment corresponding to Figure 7. Although the median values are quite low, the maximum values are relatively high as expected.

div.p: The task set generation procedure is identical to the one described in Section VII with U = 0.9. As expected, there exists a large performance gap between EDF and EPPT (or EPP) when the value of δ is small. However, both EPPT and EPP significantly outperform all the remaining algorithms across various deadline factors. To understand how the number of tasks in a task set affect the performance of EPP and EPPT, we also show the acceptance ratios of different algorithms for varying number of tasks. We generate constrained deadline task sets using the same generation strategy as the above experiment, with U = 0.9 and number of tasks n chosen from the set n ∈ {3, 6, 9, . . . , 30}. Figure 10 shows the acceptance ratios of different algorithms, and box-plot Figure 11 shows the corresponding number of tuning steps for EPPT. As we can see, EPPT continues to significantly outperform all the other algorithms, except EDF. In fact, its performance seems to be independent of the number of tasks, even increasing slightly for larger n. However, as n increases, the number of tuning steps required for EPPT to converge also increases. Although the median number of steps is relatively small and does not increase significantly with n, there are task sets with n = 30 tasks for which EPPT takes up to 52 steps to converge. However, this increase still appears to be bounded polynomially in the number of tasks n. In all the previous experiments, we set the lower bound for step-size as α min i = D i /30 and the upper bound as α max i = D i /10 in EPPT. The algorithm then selects promotion points based on Equation (15). It is then interesting to know how much the performance of EPPT depends on these bounds. We conducted a simple experiment for this purpose in which we set Δ i = 1 for each task τ i , i.e., the step-size for tuning is set to 1. EPPT would have the best possible performance with this setting because it is able to reduce promotion points by 1 time unit in each step. Figure 12 shows the acceptance ratios for three algorithms; EDF, EPPT and EPPT (max), where the last one denotes EPPT with Δ i = 1. As we can see, the performance gap between EPPT (max) and EPPT is very small. However, as expected, the number of tuning steps increase significantly (Figure 13 versus Figure 8). Therefore we can conclude that EPPT with α min i = D i /30, α max i = D i /10 and Δ i selected using Equation ( 15) offers a very good compromise between schedulability and the number of tuning steps required for convergence.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents a sufficient schedulability analysis for DP scheduling and two different heuristics EPP and EPPT to assign promotion points to the tasks. Results from a variety of experiments show that the heuristics outperform both FP scheduling and limited-preemption scheduling. This shows the power of DP scheduling to effectively exploit processing capacity, and the performance of EPPT is same as (resp. very close to) that of EDF scheduling for implicit (resp. constrained) deadline task systems.

To simplify the presentation, the proposed test has made an assumption that each task τ i has an initial priority (n + i) and a promoted priority i, where a lower number indicates higher priority. In the future, we can extend it to any other promoted priority assignment by considering additional cases. However, even with this simple priority assignment, EPPT has still exhibited good performance in terms of schedulability.
